frameworks.name: Opportunity Vehicle Assessment
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's three-factor framework for evaluating a business opportunity: (1) total number of potential units that can be sold, (2) gross margin per unit sold, and (3) supply/demand dynamics for entry — the product of all three determines opportunity quality.

frameworks.name: Front-End Launch to Legacy Continuity Stack
frameworks.definition: Sell a fixed-term high-priced front-end program (e.g., 16-week launch at $16k) to liquidate CAC, then downsell into a lower-priced recurring continuity program (e.g., $800/week legacy), framing the continuity as more value for less money.

frameworks.name: Dual-EFT Revenue Model
frameworks.definition: Sell a service-based recurring charge (EFT) and a product-based recurring charge (EFT) in the same transaction, creating two independent recurring revenue streams per customer, each with different cost structures.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch licensing business generated $25.9 million in top-line revenue and $17 million in EBITDA in its second year of operation (2017), yielding an approximately 65% EBITDA margin.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: annual business performance (year 2 of Gym Launch licensing)

bounded_by: Year 3 EBITDA declined from Year 2 despite higher top line because Hormozi split focus by launching a second company (Prestige Labs) simultaneously

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that launching a second active company while the first is still scaling is a strategic mistake, because divided focus degrades EBITDA margin even when top-line grows: Gym Launch top-line rose from $25.9M to ~$37M in Year 3, but EBITDA fell from $17M to $13.4M after he started Prestige Labs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder is the primary operational and strategic driver of the first business
Second business requires active founder attention, not passive capital deployment
claims.mechanism: Splitting founder attention between two scaling businesses degrades execution quality on both, compressing EBITDA margin even when aggregate revenue grows.

numbers.axis: EBITDA margin shift when second company launched

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that cutting the Gym Launch licensing price by 25% (from $800/week to $600/week, i.e., from $42,000/year to $31,200/year) produced no measurable reduction in churn, resulting only in direct top-line revenue loss.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B licensing product for gym owners
Price reduction motivated by anticipated acquirer preference for lower churn
claims.mechanism: Churn in this context was not driven by price sensitivity; lowering price removed revenue without addressing the real churn drivers, so the only outcome was lost margin.

numbers.axis: weekly licensing price vs. observed churn outcome

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch direct-to-consumer weight loss program achieved 70-80% success rates for participants on a 6-week challenge by structuring the offer as a wager: clients paid $500 upfront and received a full refund if they lost 20 pounds in six weeks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Direct-to-consumer weight loss, gym setting
Fixed 6-week program with measurable outcome threshold (20 lb loss)
claims.mechanism: Wagering money increases compliance because participants are motivated to avoid loss (loss aversion), raising completion and success rates far above the industry average for weight loss programs.

numbers.axis: success rate on 6-week weight loss challenge

anchors.structure: Hormozi wager offer ($500 refundable on 20 lb loss)

bounded_by: Wagers are regulated by lottery laws in many jurisdictions; Hormozi notes he was unaware of this at the time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch acquisition funnel in its peak period (circa 2014-2016) achieved a 30:1 LTV-to-CAC ratio in the first 30 days: leads cost approximately $2 on average, 50-70% of leads scheduled, roughly half showed, and the in-house sales team closed at 50% (Hormozi and his wife closed at 80%) on a $500 upfront payment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Facebook advertising circa 2013-2016, lower CPMs than current
Direct-to-consumer gym weight loss offer with wager structure
In-person point-of-sale close

numbers.axis: sales funnel conversion metrics for Gym Launch direct-to-consumer program

bounded_by: Facebook ad economics were materially better in 2013-2016; same funnel would not achieve 30:1 ratio at 2024 CPM levels

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch licensing program generated an average of $30,000 in additional cash for a licensed gym in the first 30 days after implementing the acquisition system, even though gym-owner operators underperformed Hormozi's own team (who averaged $100,000 per 21-day launch).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Gym owner licensed Gym Launch acquisition system at $16,000 front-end price
First 30 days after system implementation

numbers.axis: additional cash collected in launch period by operator type

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the optimal opportunity vehicle is evaluated on three dimensions: (1) number of potential units sellable, (2) gross margin per unit, and (3) supply/demand dynamics for a new entrant. His transition from operating gyms to licensing to gym owners was motivated by recognizing that gym ownership was a low-multiple opportunity relative to his skill level.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: High TAM and high gross margin per unit can still be unattractive if supply/demand dynamics make entry as a new competitor unfavorable (e.g., telecom)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's performance-based offer for B2B lead generation agencies — charging $5,000 upfront once (not per month) then billing only per qualified appointment that physically shows up — caused willingness-to-pay to increase approximately 4x versus a $1,500/month retainer on the same delivery scope, because prospects perceive payment-on-results as zero-risk.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B lead generation agency selling to small businesses (chiropractors, local service businesses)
Offer benchmarked against a $1,500/month retainer baseline
claims.mechanism: Switching from time-based to outcome-based pricing eliminates the buyer's perceived risk of paying for no results; buyers rationally pay 4x more per outcome than per month because the risk of non-delivery is transferred to the seller.

numbers.axis: willingness to pay per show appointment vs. retainer model

bounded_by: Requires seller to have operational confidence in delivery; fail rate on lead quality destroys economics if show-rate is low

claims.text: Alex Hormozi believes that sales training materials (books, courses) should be consumed after initial selling attempts, not before, because conceptual knowledge about rapport, objection handling, and closing cannot be operationalized until the learner has experienced the deficiency firsthand.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to sales skill acquisition specifically
Learner has no prior sales experience
claims.mechanism: Concepts like rapport can only be understood after experiencing the absence of rapport; without the reference experience, knowledge cannot be bucketed into actionable categories and remains inert.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch licensing model avoided the financial failure mode of the original gym-rescue performance model (which generated ~$150,000 in refunds from 3 facilities in a short period) because the licensing model gave Hormozi upfront cash from the front-end purchase while placing fulfillment responsibility on the gym owner rather than on Hormozi's team.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Performance-based model: Hormozi's team ran campaigns and collected 100% of upfront cash from clients
Post-campaign fulfillment left to struggling gym operators who could not maintain service quality
claims.mechanism: When the party collecting cash upfront is not also responsible for ongoing fulfillment, a gap emerges between what was sold and what is delivered; this gap generates refund cascades, especially when operators communicate with each other and discover the same refund path.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi structured his Gym Launch front-end offer so that the $16,000 launch fee would be recouped by the gym owner within the first 30 days from incremental cash collected (~$30,000 average), making the ROI argument self-evident and the sale near-automatic.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B licensing offer to gym owners
Front-end price: $16,000 for 16-week implementation program
claims.mechanism: When the cost of an offer is recouped with positive margin within 30 days of purchase, the buyer's perceived risk collapses and objection volume drops sharply; the offer sells itself on ROI alone.

numbers.axis: time to ROI on $16,000 front-end licensing fee

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that customers should be sold continuity or upsells at the moment of peak excitement — before they have experienced the friction of the work — because perceived value of a program is highest before first contact with effort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Consumer health/fitness programs where the effort required becomes apparent after first session
Applies to any offer where post-purchase reality involves work or discomfort
claims.mechanism: Excitement about outcomes (the bikini in Maui) is highest pre-effort; once the customer encounters the physical difficulty (the airport, the TSA line), their motivation and willingness to pay decline. Capturing commitment before the friction experience locks in value at its maximum.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi deliberately priced the Gym Launch continuity product (Legacy program at $800/week) as a downsell from the front-end launch price ($16,000 for 16 weeks = $1,000/week), framing the continuity as more value for less money, which eliminated the psychological resistance to a recurring commitment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Customer has just completed or is near the end of a high-priced fixed-term program
Continuity offer is positioned relative to the front-end price, not relative to zero
claims.mechanism: Anchoring the continuity price against the higher front-end price makes the lower recurring price feel like a discount; the customer's mental reference point is the price they just paid, not market alternatives.

numbers.axis: price per week across program stages

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's Prestige Labs supplement drop-ship model for Gym Launch gyms generated $1.7 million in its first full launch month (January 2019) by monetizing an existing base of ~800 active gyms through a zero-inventory affiliate model paying 40% commission.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Existing B2B client base of ~800 active gym-owner licensees
Drop-ship model: no inventory held by gym; Amazon-style direct-to-consumer fulfillment via kiosk with affiliate link
40% commission paid to gyms on supplement sales
bounded_by: Revenue underperformed Hormozi's pre-launch projection (estimated $1M/week if all 800 gyms sold $5,000/month each)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that many Gym Launch licensed gyms earned more net profit from supplement resale than from their core training service, because supplement gross margin was near 100% for the gym (after the 40% affiliate commission was factored in as cost-of-sale) while service gross margin was much lower.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Gym owner operating with Gym Launch licensing system
Supplement sold via drop-ship kiosk with 40% affiliate commission, no inventory cost
claims.mechanism: The supplement sale required no recurring operational input from the gym after the initial sign-up; the affiliate commission was earned on autopilot (~$80/month per subscriber) while service delivery required ongoing labor, creating a structural margin advantage for the product stream.

numbers.axis: net margin profile by revenue type for Gym Launch gyms

anchors.margin: ~$80/month gross to gym, near 100% net for gym

examples.text: During Hormozi's gym-rescue phase, he and his team would fly into a gym, run a 21-day marketing blitz collecting 100% of upfront cash (averaging $100,000 per gym), then leave. The gym owner — who had been struggling before Hormozi arrived — would then face 150+ new members they could not fulfill at the promised quality level. Three facilities coordinated with each other, offered refunds to members if they signed directly with the gym at a lower price, and Hormozi absorbed approximately $150,000 in refunds while already having incurred full flight, hotel, sales team, and ad costs. This forced-refund cascade is what led Hormozi to abandon the performance model and transition to a licensing fee model where the gym owner bore fulfillment risk.

When Hormozi was about to cancel on eight gym owners who had signed up for the now-abandoned performance model, the first gym owner described refinancing his house and maxing out credit cards to be ready. Hormozi relented and offered to sell him the know-how instead of executing it for him. When the owner asked how much, Hormozi — trying to get a 'no' so he could avoid the commitment — said $6,000. The owner immediately agreed. Hormozi then called the next gym and quoted $8,000 for the same thing. This accidental price discovery became the Gym Launch licensing business, which went on to do $25.9M in year two.

Hormozi's Gym Launch consumer weight loss funnel stacked multiple revenue events in sequence within 30 days: Day 0 — collect $500 upfront for 6-week challenge. Day 1 — complimentary nutrition consultation where ~$200 in supplements (creatine, pre-workout) was sold per ticket. Week 3 — when the member had lost ~12 pounds, a conversation redirected focus from the 6-week goal to a long-year goal, then enrolled them in a year-long membership at a discounted rate, funded by spreading their $500 challenge payment over 12 months (yielding ~$199/month net). Week 6 — upsell to semi-private 1-on-4 training at higher ticket. This created two separate EFTs (service recurring + product recurring) from a single $500 front-end acquisition.

Hormozi ran a pricing survey to his lead-generation agency customers asking two questions: (1) if his team worked their leads, what would they pay as a flat monthly rate? and (2) what would they pay per qualified show (same scope, pay-on-result framing)? Seventy-five percent of respondents said they'd pay $300-$400/month for the flat service. For pay-per-show framing, willingness to pay was approximately 4x higher. Hormozi used this survey data to redesign his agency offer from a monthly retainer to a pay-per-show model, capturing the 4x WTP premium while making the offer easier to sell because the chiropractor or local business owner perceived zero risk of paying for no results.

practices.text: When designing a licensing or franchise-style model, collect the front-end program fee as a lump sum upfront large enough to cover the cost of customer acquisition and implementation support, so you never need external capital to fund growth.

When building a sales training program for operators or new hires, create it as short as possible — only enough to get someone from zero to their first close (e.g., 2 hours for a new rep to close $500 deals on day one) rather than comprehensive enough to feel complete.

After a customer completes a fixed-term program, always have a continuity offer framed as 'more value for less cost than what you just paid' by anchoring it against the completed program's per-unit price rather than against a zero baseline.
Before reading sales books or taking sales courses, go sell first to accumulate real objection experiences; then revisit training materials to match concepts to situations already encountered.
